extracted.intended_audience: state permitting authorities, EPA staff, regulated electric generating unit owners/operators, and public commenters
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory preamble language describing how New Source Performance Standards (NSPS), New Source Review (NSR) (PSD and NNSR), Title V, and related analyses (RIA, SC-GHG, CGE) should be interpreted and applied for fossil fuel-fired electric generating units, including public participation and environmental justice considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide opportunity for a public hearing (CAA 165(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Permitting authority must “[p]rovide opportunity for a public hearing for interested persons to appear and submit written or oral comments on the air quality impact of the source, alternatives to it, the control technology required, and other appropriate considerations.” (40 CFR 51.166(q)(2)(v))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The quoted scope—air quality impact, alternatives, control technology, and other appropriate considerations—can be interpreted broadly to include issues raised by commenters (e.g., need for a facility). Public hearing opportunities are a required element of the permitting process under PSD regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enhance environmental justice by increasing public participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Permitting authorities should provide opportunities to enhance environmental justice by facilitating increased public participation in the formal permit consideration process (e.g., by granting requests to extend public comment periods, holding multiple public meetings, or providing translation services at hearings in areas with limited English proficiency).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitting authorities can also take informal steps earlier in the process, such as inviting community groups to meet with the permitting authority and express concerns before a draft permit is issued, to ensure meaningful public engagement and EJ consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitting discretion to incorporate siting/EJ concerns and impose conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The “alternatives” and “other appropriate considerations” language in CAA 165(a)(2) can be interpreted to provide the permitting authority with discretion to incorporate siting and environmental justice considerations when issuing PSD permits—specifically, to impose permit conditions on the basis of environmental justice considerations raised in public comments regarding the air quality impacts of a proposed source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (EAB) recognition that consideration of the need for a facility is within scope when raised by a commenter supports this discretion. Permitting authorities should document the basis for any such decisions in the permit record.

rubrics_metrics.name: BACT requirement for PSD permits
rubrics_metrics.description: For PSD permits, the permitting authority must establish emission limitations based on BACT for each pollutant that is subject to PSD at the new major stationary source or at each emissions unit involved in the major modification. BACT is assessed on a case-by-case basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The BACT analysis evaluates the emission reductions each available control technology/technique would achieve and the energy, environmental, economic, and other costs associated with each technology or technique. BACT cannot be less stringent than any applicable standard of performance under the NSPS.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA five-step 'top-down' approach for BACT
rubrics_metrics.description: Many permitting authorities apply EPA's five-step 'top-down' approach to ensure all BACT criteria are considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps: (1) identify all available control options that have potential for practical application for the regulated NSR pollutant and emissions unit; (2) eliminate options that are technically infeasible; (3) rank remaining options from most to least effective; (4) evaluate energy, environmental, economic impacts, and other costs and eliminate options not achievable based on these considerations from the top down; (5) select the most effective remaining option as BACT.

rubrics_metrics.name: BACT scope and 'redefining the source' limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The list of available control options need not necessarily include inherently lower-polluting processes that would fundamentally redefine the nature of the source proposed by the permit applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BACT generally should not regulate the applicant's purpose or objective for the facility, but permitting authorities have discretion to conduct a broader analysis and consider options that change aspects of facility design. Any decision to exclude an option on 'redefining the source' grounds should be explained and documented in the permit record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider collateral environmental and EJ impacts in BACT cost-effectiveness analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: In analyzing energy, environmental, and economic impacts of each control option, permitting authorities may consider a wide variety of environmental impacts (e.g., solid/hazardous waste generation, water discharges, visibility impacts, local water demand, emissions of other pollutants such as air toxics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitting authorities have discretion in the form of BACT analysis and weight given to impacts; authorities may place more weight on collateral environmental effects on local communities (e.g., if co-pollutant increases disproportionately affect minority or low-income populations), which could lead to eliminating more stringent controls in favor of less stringent technologies with more acceptable collateral impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of offsite lifecycle impacts in control option evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: The BACT analysis may extend to considering reduced or excessive energy or environmental impacts of the control alternative at an offsite location that supports the operation of the facility obtaining the permit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a permitting authority may weigh favorably a control option involving co-firing with hydrogen produced from low-GHG processes (e.g., electrolysis powered by renewables) to recognize reduced environmental impact of producing the fuel for the control option.

rubrics_metrics.name: LAER requirement for NNSR permits
rubrics_metrics.description: For NNSR (nonattainment) permits, LAER is defined as the most stringent emission limitation required under a SIP or achieved in practice for a class or category of sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike BACT, LAER does not consider economic, energy, or other environmental factors—except that LAER is not considered achievable if cost is so great that a major new stationary source could not be built or operated. As with BACT, a determination of LAER cannot be less stringent than any applicable NSPS.

rubrics_metrics.name: NSPS as a minimum for BACT but BACT may be more stringent
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an NSPS applies to a new or reconstructed EGU, that NSPS serves as the minimum level of control in determining BACT for major NSR applicability for sources commencing construction after the proposed NSPS publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The existence of an NSPS minimum does not preclude a permitting authority from selecting a more stringent control for the PSD permit or considering control technologies beyond those considered when developing the NSPS. BACT authority is separate from BSER and requires a case-by-case, source-specific review that can reflect advances in control technology, cost reductions, or other relevant information since the NSPS was issued.

rubrics_metrics.name: State plans/emission guidelines and NSR interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Under emission guidelines, each state develops a plan establishing standards of performance for affected EGUs; when a stationary source undertakes a physical or operational change (including to comply with a state plan), the source may need to obtain a preconstruction NSR permit depending on emissions increases and local attainment status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because emission guidelines are intended to reduce emissions at existing sources, a NSR permit may not be needed if the change will not increase emissions. States may design plans to avoid triggering major NSR (e.g., by developing enforceable conditions that effectively limit a unit's ability to increase emissions—creating a synthetic minor limitation). States may also adopt other strategies to preserve operational flexibility (e.g., for base load units) while avoiding unintended NSR triggers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title V permit requirements and permit reopening timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Title V permits must include emission limitations and standards, including operational requirements and limitations that assure compliance with all applicable requirements; requirements resulting from these rules that are imposed on EGUs with Title V permits are applicable requirements and must be incorporated into the source's Title V permit per the Title V regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a permit has a remaining life of 3 years or more, a permit reopening to incorporate the newly applicable requirement shall be completed no later than 18 months after promulgation of the applicable requirement. If the permit has a remaining life of less than 3 years, the newly applicable requirement must be incorporated at permit renewal. Reopening proceedings follow the same procedures as initial permit issuance, only affect parts with cause to reopen, and should be expeditious. States may label provisions as 'state-only' or 'not federally enforceable' until EPA approval of a state plan to ensure meaningful public participation during plan development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Impact Analysis (RIA) is separate from BSER and must follow OMB/EPA guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: RIA prepared in accordance with E.O. 12866, E.O. 13563, OMB Circular A-4, and the EPA's Guidelines for Preparing Economic Analyses presents expected economic consequences (benefits, costs) for illustrative scenarios; the RIA is separate from the statutory BSER determinations and did not influence choice of BSER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RIA presents PV and EAV of costs/benefits for 2024–2047 (discounted to 2019 dollars) and snapshot years (2028, 2030, 2035, 2040, 2045). It includes analyses of economic, energy, environmental justice, and employment impacts, uses discount rates (2%, 3%, 7%), and acknowledges uncertainty because states have flexibility in plan design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of CGE (SAGE) modeling for economy-wide impacts with limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA used a CGE model called SAGE to evaluate potential economy-wide impacts of the final rules; the SAB recommended integrating CGE modeling into regulatory analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SAGE was peer-reviewed; it provides annualized social cost estimates (e.g., $1.32B annualized social cost between 2024–2047 at a 4.5% discount) but currently does not estimate emissions changes nor account for environmental benefits. The RIA uses SAGE alongside other models and responds to reviewer and comment suggestions for sensitivity analyses and future improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and update of Social Cost of Greenhouse Gases (SC-GHG)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA estimates climate benefits using SC-GHG that reflect recent advances in the scientific literature and incorporate National Academies' recommendations; SC-GHG is the monetary value of the net harm to society from a marginal increase in GHG emissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The SC-GHG should, in principle, include many types of climate impacts (agriculture, human health, property damage, energy system disruption, conflict risk, ecosystem services), but data and modeling limitations mean some impacts are omitted, leading to partial accounting and likely underestimation. EPA participates in the IWG process, solicits public comment, and uses external peer review and sensitivity analyses when applying updated estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetized benefits analysis is for E.O. 12866 comparisons and distinct from BSER
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA monetizes climate and health benefits to enable benefit-cost comparisons pursuant to E.O. 12866, but the monetized benefits analysis is entirely distinct from the statutory BSER determinations and was not relied upon to determine standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA recognizes substantial uncertainties and limitations in monetizing benefits (including unquantified benefits). The RIA presents projected PV and EAV estimates for climate and health benefits under different discounting assumptions and explicitly states how monetized benefits are used for regulatory review rather than standard-setting.
